column1: auth-code|How should a browser-based application use OAuth authorization code flow securely?|Redirect to a trusted authorization endpoint, bind the transaction to the browser session, use authorization code plus PKCE, and validate redirect URI and issuer expectations. Exchange the one-time code securely. OAuth authorization alone is not proof of user identity; use OpenID Connect for authentication claims.|code;PKCE;redirect;OpenID~identity|OAuth authorization itself proves a user's identity.|A SPA wants to use an implicit flow because it cannot keep a client secret. What is the safer modern design?|Use authorization code with PKCE; a public client need not invent a shared secret. Consider a backend-for-frontend to keep long-lived tokens away from browser JavaScript and validate transaction bindings.|oauth-bcp|PKCE

pkce|What does PKCE protect, and how does S256 work?|Generate a high-entropy verifier per authorization transaction and send its base64url-encoded SHA-256 challenge with the authorization request. Present the original verifier at code exchange. This binds an intercepted code to the initiating client; it does not replace all redirect, issuer, or browser protections.|verifier;challenge;SHA-256~S256;code|PKCE is a permanent shared client secret.|An attacker steals an authorization code but not its verifier. Why should token exchange fail?|The authorization server recomputes the verifier's challenge and compares it with the one bound to the code. A mismatched verifier must not redeem that code.|pkce|code_verifier

access-refresh|How do access tokens and refresh tokens differ?|An access token authorizes resource-server requests and should be scoped and short-lived. A refresh token obtains replacement access tokens from the authorization server and needs stronger storage, rotation, revocation, and replay protection. Token format and lifetime are separate choices.|resource~API;refresh;scope~lifetime|A refresh token should be sent to every resource API.|A mobile client receives an expired access token. Should it replay the refresh token against the business API?|No. Use the authorization server's refresh endpoint according to the client flow, then retry with the replacement access token under bounded policies.|oauth-bcp|refresh token

jwt-validation|Which checks are required when accepting a signed JWT as an access token?|Verify the signature using trusted keys and a configured allowed algorithm, then validate issuer, audience, expiry, and any required not-before or token-type constraints. Decoding is not verification; do not trust an attacker-supplied key URL or algorithm choice blindly.|signature;issuer;audience;expir|Base64-decoding a JWT proves its signature is valid.|A service decodes a JWT and trusts its role claim without checking the signature. Explain the vulnerability and fix.|An attacker can forge claims. Verify with trusted issuer keys and allowed algorithms, validate audience and time claims, then enforce server-side authorization on the requested resource.|jwt|audience

revocation|Can a signed JWT be revoked immediately without any server-side checks?|A self-contained JWT accepted offline normally remains usable until expiry. Immediate revocation requires a denylist, session/version check, introspection, key policy, or another stateful mechanism. Short access-token lifetimes reduce but do not eliminate the revocation window.|expiry~expir;denylist~introspection~stateful;window|Deleting a browser JWT immediately invalidates every stolen copy.|A stolen access JWT is still accepted after logout. Design a stronger revocation policy.|Invalidate refresh/session state, keep access lifetimes short, and add server-side revocation or session-version checks when immediate termination is required. Explain the availability and lookup-cost tradeoff.|jwt,oauth-bcp|expiration

refresh-rotation|How does refresh-token rotation help detect replay?|Issue a new refresh token on use and invalidate the previous one, tracking the token family or equivalent relationship. Reuse of an invalidated token can indicate compromise and trigger revocation. Concurrent legitimate refresh attempts need an explicit race policy.|new~rotate;invalidate~previous;reuse~replay;family~race|Rotation means old refresh tokens remain valid forever.|Two browser tabs refresh concurrently and one token is reported reused. What must the implementation account for?|Serialize refreshes or define a carefully bounded concurrency policy; distinguish expected races without allowing unlimited replay, and revoke compromised token families when reuse is confirmed.|oauth-bcp|rotation

cookies|What do HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite cookies protect against?|HttpOnly prevents normal JavaScript from reading the cookie, Secure restricts transmission to secure contexts, and SameSite limits certain cross-site cookie sending. These flags mitigate different threats; HttpOnly alone neither prevents CSRF nor stops an active XSS script from issuing authenticated actions.|HttpOnly;Secure;SameSite;CSRF~XSS|HttpOnly alone prevents all CSRF and XSS attacks.|A session cookie is HttpOnly but a malicious cross-site form performs a state change. Why can this happen?|Cookie readability is unrelated to automatic cookie attachment. Add CSRF defenses such as validated tokens or origin checks and appropriate SameSite policy; keep authorization checks server-side.|owasp-session,owasp-csrf|HttpOnly

csrf|When is a synchronizer token or equivalent CSRF defense needed?|When browsers attach credentials automatically, cross-site state-changing requests can abuse them. Validate an unpredictable session-bound CSRF token or an appropriate signed double-submit design, check origins as defense in depth, and avoid unsafe state changes on GET. SameSite is not a universal replacement.|cookie~credential;token;origin~SameSite;GET|Using HTTPS alone stops CSRF.|A JSON API uses cookie authentication and enables credentialed cross-origin requests. Does JSON alone guarantee CSRF protection?|No universal guarantee. Review accepted content types, CORS policy, preflight behavior, and credential handling; retain deliberate CSRF protections and exact allowed origins.|owasp-csrf|token

xss|Why is output encoding contextual, and what does CSP add?|Encode untrusted data for the destination context: HTML text, attributes, URLs, and JavaScript have different rules. Prefer safe DOM APIs and sanitize permitted HTML. CSP adds defense in depth but does not repair unsafe string interpolation or replace encoding.|context;encod~safe DOM;CSP~sanitize|One generic escape function makes every JavaScript and HTML context safe.|A name is HTML-escaped and then inserted into an inline JavaScript string. Is that sufficient?|No. HTML encoding is not JavaScript-string encoding. Avoid inline script construction and use safe structured data transfer or APIs appropriate to the exact context.|owasp-xss|context

localstorage|What are the security trade-offs of storing bearer tokens in localStorage?|JavaScript can read localStorage, so XSS can exfiltrate bearer tokens. HttpOnly cookies reduce that read exposure but are automatically attached and require CSRF considerations. Choose storage and architecture from the threat model rather than claiming any browser storage is universally safe.|XSS;JavaScript;HttpOnly~CSRF;threat|localStorage protects tokens from JavaScript-based XSS.|A team moves a session token to localStorage solely to solve CSRF. Review the decision.|That changes the attack surface rather than eliminating risk: bearer-token theft through XSS becomes central. Compare a backend session or BFF design, short lifetimes, and strong XSS/CSRF controls.|owasp-session|localStorage

authorization|Why must RBAC and object-level authorization be enforced at the server boundary?|Authentication identifies a principal; authorization decides permitted actions on specific resources. Validate role and tenant/object access on each server-side request, deny by default, and do not trust UI visibility or client-provided tenant identifiers.|authentication;server;tenant~object;deny|Hiding an admin button is a sufficient authorization boundary.|An ordinary user changes /documents/123 to /documents/124 and reads another tenant's record. What check is missing?|A resource-level authorization check bound to authenticated tenant and principal. A valid login and broad user role alone are insufficient.|owasp-authz|every request

webhook-signature|How should a GitHub-style webhook signature be verified?|Compute the expected HMAC over the exact raw request bytes using the configured secret, select the correct signature scheme, and compare in constant time after validating lengths. Parse or act on the body only after verification; reserialized JSON changes the signed bytes.|HMAC;raw;constant~timing;secret|Parsing and reserializing JSON preserves every webhook signature.|A middleware parses a webhook body before signature validation and legitimate signatures fail. Repair the boundary.|Capture the original raw bytes for HMAC validation. Do not verify a reserialized object. Enforce body size limits, secret rotation policy, and failed-signature handling.|webhooks|HMAC

replay|Does a valid webhook HMAC by itself prevent replay?|No. A captured authentic payload may be replayed. When the sender signs timestamps, enforce a bounded freshness window; also record delivery or event identifiers with suitable retention and idempotent processing. Timestamp fields must be covered by authentication to be trustworthy.|replay;timestamp~freshness;delivery~identifier;idempot|A valid HMAC alone proves a request has never been seen before.|An attacker resends an authentic signed event ten times. How do you stop duplicate side effects?|Deduplicate a trusted delivery/event identifier atomically and make the handler idempotent. Apply a timestamp window if supported by the signed protocol; do not assume all providers sign timestamps.|webhooks,aws-idempotency|signature

idempotency-key|What makes an idempotency-key implementation safe under concurrent requests?|Scope the key to the authenticated operation or tenant, store a request fingerprint and result, and claim the key atomically with the business mutation or equivalent state machine. Reuse the stored outcome for the same request and reject conflicting payload reuse. Define expiry and in-progress recovery.|atomic~transaction;payload~fingerprint;result~outcome;tenant~scope|A random idempotency key alone prevents duplicate database mutations.|Two identical requests with the same key arrive simultaneously and both pass a check-before-insert. Fix the race.|Use a unique constraint or atomic claim inside the transaction/state machine, associate payload and result, and reconcile crashes. A non-atomic existence check is insufficient.|aws-idempotency|idempotent

tenant-boundary|How should a multi-tenant API derive the tenant for authorization?|Derive authorized tenant membership from the authenticated principal and trusted server-side policy, then scope every relevant query, cache key, and background task. Client headers can select among allowed tenants but cannot grant membership. Test cross-tenant access explicitly.|principal~membership;server;query~cache;cross-tenant|A client-supplied tenant header is sufficient proof of membership.|A background job receives only tenant_id and document_id from a client. What additional checks and state are needed?|Validate the authenticated enqueueing principal's access, persist trusted job scope, and enforce tenant filters again during processing. Do not turn an untrusted identifier into an authorization grant.|owasp-authz,postgres-rls|tenant
